_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 2 Mathematics unit lecture film, Lesson 9 Count It, Chart It. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow the lesson opener's three parts (sorting and tallying; charts and pictograms; likely or random) opened out with the lesson page's own steps: Sort them into groups (fruit or vegetable), Ask collect answer and Tally charts, Build and Reading a block graph, Pictograms and Spot the mistake's key of 2, Sorting two ways (the Carroll diagram, red and round), and Toss a coin with Regular or random. One set of numbers runs through the whole film: mango 8, banana 5, orange 4, seventeen children in all, and a coin run of six heads and four tails.
title: Count It, Chart It
subtitle: Grade 2 Mathematics
objectives: Conduct an investigation to answer non-statistical and statistical questions (categorical data).

Record, organise and represent categorical data. Choose and explain which representation to use in a given situation: lists and tables Venn and Carroll diagrams tally charts block graphs and pictograms.
Describe data, identifying similarities and variations to answer non-statistical and statistical questions and discuss conclusions.
Use familiar language associated with patterns and randomness, including regular pattern and random pattern.
Conduct chance experiments with two outcomes, and present and describe the results.

beats.say: Ask a question. Count what people say. Then show it.
A tally, a block graph and a pictogram all do that job.
Sorting puts things that are alike together. It needs one clear rule.
Here the rule is fruit, or vegetable. Nothing else matters.
An apple is a fruit, so it goes here. A carrot is a vegetable.
Each thing goes in one hoop only. Sort by the rule, not by colour.
An investigation starts with a question you want answered.
Which fruit do you like best? Ask everyone in your class.

at.which: Which fruit do you like best

beats.say: Make one mark for every answer you hear. Do it straight away.
Every fifth mark goes across the other four. That bundle is five.
Mango got a gate of five, and three more. That is eight.
Now show your counts on a block graph. One block is one child.
Count the blocks, do not guess. The mango column reaches eight.
Banana has five blocks. Orange has four. They start on one line.
Mango is tallest, so most children chose mango.
Eight take away five is three, so three more chose mango.
A pictogram shows the same counts using pictures instead of blocks.
Here one picture is one child, so you just count the pictures.
But always read the key first. Here one picture stands for two children.
Walk has four pictures. Two, four, six, eight: that is eight children.
A Carroll diagram sorts things two ways at once. Check both labels.
Across the top it says red, or not red.
Down the side it says round, or not round.
An apple is red and round, so it goes in the box where both are true.

at.box: the box where both are true

beats.say: A coin can land two ways, heads or tails. Toss it ten times.
This run gave six heads and four tails. Six and four make ten.
Heads, tails, heads, tails keeps repeating. That is a regular pattern.
Your real tosses have no repeat anywhere. That is a random pattern.
So nobody can say how the next toss will land. Heads is not due.
You sorted by one rule, and kept a tally in fives.
You read a block graph, and a pictogram with its key.
A Carroll diagram sorts two ways at once.
And you can tell a regular pattern from a random one.
